description: Hi! I’m a 2nd-year Biomedical Sciences student (CET) from the Netherlands, and welcome to CareScreen! We’re building a practical visual health monitor that translates astronaut health data into clear, actionable guidance. I bring the biomedical knowledge, while keeping our direction open to brainstorm together. Everyone is welcome, whether you’re into coding, design, video, or just love space. Let’s build something great!

By switching between activities, such as an extravehicular activity (EVA) and habitat maintenance, astronauts can explore how the same health profile may have different implications depending on the physical and environmental demands involved. details:
CareScreen

CareScreen is a mission-aware astronaut health interpretation tool designed to help astronauts understand how their current health relates to the demands of their upcoming mission activities. While conventional health monitoring systems primarily present individual measurements, such as heart rate, sleep quality and activity levels, CareScreen places these measurements in the context of the mission ahead. Its central question is: How might an astronaut's current health status affect the mission they are about to perform?

Functionality and workflow

CareScreen is designed to integrate health monitoring into existing mission preparation and debriefing routines through a check-in/check-out approach. Before an activity, astronauts review their current health profile and select their upcoming mission activity, such as an extravehicular activity (EVA) or habitat maintenance. The system considers the demands of that activity alongside individual health baselines, recent trends, recovery indicators and environmental exposure to provide a mission-specific interpretation.

After the activity, a check-out provides an opportunity to review post-mission health, fatigue, symptoms and perceived recovery. Over time, information from these check-ins and check-outs could help identify individual patterns in how astronauts respond to different mission activities. This approach aims to fit into existing astronaut workflows rather than requiring continuous interaction with another monitoring system.

Health dimensions and visualisation

The system brings together five interconnected health dimensions: cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, immune, neuro-ocular, and behavioural and cognitive health. These dimensions are represented through a centralised dashboard, combining individual health profiles, baseline and trend information, and an overview of relevant environmental factors.

Each health dimension has its own consistent colour, making it easier to distinguish and recognise different areas of health throughout the interface. A central feature is the radar chart, which visualises the relative relevance of each health dimension to the selected mission activity. Its five axes represent the five dimensions, while the filled shape changes according to the demands of the selected activity. For example, an EVA and habitat maintenance place different demands on the astronaut, resulting in different visual interpretations of the same health profile. Importantly, changing the selected activity changes the mission-related interpretation, not the underlying health measurements.

The radar chart also distinguishes mission relevance from deviations from an individual's personal baseline. The blended colour at its centre combines the five dimension colours according to their relative relevance. It serves as a visual summary rather than a health score, diagnosis or direct measurement. The interface uses a dark, high-contrast design and a clear visual hierarchy to make complex information easier to navigate and interpret.

Scientific foundation and design considerations

The concept was informed by research from NASA's Human Research Program and the Canadian Space Agency. Our research highlighted individual variability in responses to spaceflight, interactions between physiological and behavioural systems, and the importance of adaptation, recovery and personalised monitoring. We considered how factors such as sleep, fatigue, environmental exposure and mission workload can influence multiple health dimensions simultaneously.

We also considered the limitations of current spaceflight health research, particularly the need for objective and subjective measurements, individual baselines, and astronaut-specific reference values. Not all health changes can be interpreted using universal thresholds. Therefore, CareScreen focuses on contextualising health information rather than relying exclusively on isolated measurements or fixed thresholds.

Creativity, development and intended impact

The main innovation of CareScreen is treating mission activities as part of the health interpretation process itself. Instead of simply displaying health metrics, it connects an astronaut's health profile to the operational demands ahead. This allows the same health information to have different implications depending on the selected activity. Its workflow-oriented approach, combination of five health dimensions and visual mission-specific interpretation aim to reduce the cognitive effort required to understand complex health information.

The interactive prototype was developed using HTML, with Claude supporting the development process, and hosted through GitHub Pages. It currently uses simulated data to demonstrate the interface, visualisations and mission-selection functionality. Further development could incorporate real health-monitoring data, more extensive pre- and post-mission comparisons, and individual adaptation profiles that learn from previous mission responses.

Ultimately, CareScreen aims to support astronaut autonomy, improve mission-related health awareness and encourage informed decisions, including consultation with mission medical support when appropriate. Its broader ambition is to contribute to more personalised health management during future long-duration lunar and Mars missions.

For prototyping Claude AI was used for code.
